games.title: Myerson (1991), Figure 4.2
games.description:
An example which illustrates the distinction between
an equilibrium of an extensive form game and an equilibrium of its
(multi)agent representation.  The actions B1, Z1, and W2 form a
behavior profile which is an equilibrium in the (multi)agent
representation.  However, it is not a Nash equilibrium of the extensive
game, because Player 1 would prefer to switch from (B1, Z1) to
(A1, Y1); the (multi)agent representation rules out such coordinated
deviations across information sets.

games.title: Watson (2013), Exercise 29.6
games.description:
A signaling game based on a scene from the Rob Reiner film, The Princess Bride:

Wesley (the protagonist) confronts the evil prince Humperdinck.  Wesley
is one of two types: weak or strong.  Wesley knows whether he is weak or
strong, but the prince only knows that he is weak with probability 1/2 and
strong with probability 1/2.  Wesley is lying in a bed in the prince's
castle when the prince enters the room.  Wesley decides whether to get out
of bed or stay in bed.  The prince observes Wesley's action but does not
observe Wesley's type.  The prince then decides whether to fight or
surrender to Wesley.  The payoffs are such that the prince prefers to fight
only with the weak Wesley, because otherwise the prince is an inferior
swordsman.  Also, the weak Wesley must pay a cost to get out of bed.

In the game in this file, the cost the weak Wesley pays to get out of bed
is set to 2.

games.title: Jakobsen et al. (2016), Figure 3
games.description:
The extensive form of an onion routing game that is not exactly timeable.
Chance chooses a sender by drawing a signal from {0, 1, 2, 3} with equal probability.
The sender does not make a strategic choice; only the two intermediary players act.
For signal i:
(a) the sender is the player whose index (mod 4) equals i,
(b) the recipient is the player whose index (mod 4) equals i-1.
The first intermediary is Player i+2 (mod 4) and the second is Player i+1.
The full mapping is as follows:
Signal 0: Player 4 sends to Player 3.  Player 2 acts first, then Player 1.
Signal 1: Player 1 sends to Player 4.  Player 3 acts first, then Player 2.
Signal 2: Player 2 sends to Player 1.  Player 4 acts first, then Player 3.
Signal 3: Player 3 sends to Player 2.  Player 1 acts first, then Player 4.
Each player has one information set with two member nodes, that is, they cannot distinguish which position they are at.
Each intermediary chooses to either forward the envelope or obstruct by keeping it.
Each player wants to obstruct the protocol if they are the first intermediary, but wants to help if they are the second.
If both intermediaries forward, the message is delivered.
In that case, the first intermediary receives -1 and the second intermediary receives 1+epsilon.
All other players receive 0.
If either intermediary obstructs, the message is not delivered and all players receive 0.
With epsilon set to 0.01, the payoffs for successful delivery are:
Signal 0: (1.01, -1, 0, 0).
Signal 1: (0, 1.01, -1, 0).
Signal 2: (0, 0, 1.01, -1).
Signal 3: (-1, 0, 0, 1.01).

games.title: Banks and Sobel (1987), Figure 1
games.description:
A sequential settlement game, a signaling game in which the Sender is a defendant of type t1 (not negligent) or t2 (negligent) and the Receiver is the plaintiff. The Sender offers a low settlement m1 or a high settlement m2, and the Receiver accepts (a1) or rejects (a2). The paper tabulates payoffs by message, with one bimatrix for each message, a row for each type and a column for each Receiver action. This file enters them as an extensive game: chance chooses the type, the Sender chooses a message, and the Receiver chooses an action at one information set for each message.

There are two kinds of sequential equilibria. In one, both types offer m1 and the Receiver accepts any offer. In the other, both types offer m2 and the Receiver accepts m2 and rejects m1, which requires the Receiver to believe, after m1, that the Sender is type t1 with probability at most 2/5. The paper rejects the second as implausible: t1 prefers to defect whenever t2 does, so after m1 the relative probability of t1 should increase. The prior is that each type has probability 1/2.

source.title: Equilibrium selection in signaling games

games.title: Banks and Sobel (1987), Figure 3
games.description:
A signaling game with a universally divine equilibrium that is not stable. The paper tabulates payoffs by message, with one bimatrix for each message, a row for each type and a column for each Receiver action; this file enters them as an extensive game in which chance chooses the type, the Sender chooses a message, and the Receiver chooses an action at one information set for each message (message m1 allows only the action a). The prior is that t1 has probability 2/5 (the paper writes .4).

There is a sequential equilibrium in which both types send m1 and the Receiver responds to m2 with a1, supported by the belief that t1 sent m2 with probability at least 2/3. It is universally divine but not stable. The stable equilibrium has both types sending m2, with the Receiver responding with a3. The game motivates the notion of stable beliefs.

source.title: Equilibrium selection in signaling games

Its Nash equilibria form a single connected component; the paper's stable set contains the equilibria (T,(1/4,3/4)) and (T,(3/4,1/4)).

The paper calls this game :math:`\Delta`. Player I's strategies are T, M and B; player II's are L and R.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 1
games.description:
A perfect-information game showing that not every Nash equilibrium is strategically stable. The profile (T,R) is a Nash equilibrium, but even though communication is impossible, player II will deviate to L whenever he has to move, which upsets it; the backwards induction equilibrium is (M,L).

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or M, which gives II the move; II then chooses L or R.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 10

Player I chooses T, which ends the game with payoffs (1,-1), or continue; he then chooses M or B; player II, not told which, chooses L or R. The payoffs are those of the matrix game :math:`\Delta`.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 11
games.description:
A three-player game, suggested by Faruk Gul, showing that a stable set can contain equilibria from different connected components of the Nash equilibria and give different payoffs from the unique sequential equilibrium. The set {(T,L,l), (T,R,r)} is stable and gives the payoffs (2,0,0), whereas the unique sequential equilibrium is ((0,1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(1/2,1/2)), with payoffs (11/4,5/4,5/4).

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or continue; he then chooses M or B. Player II, not told which, chooses L or R, and player III, told neither choice, chooses l or r.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 12
games.description:
A perfect-information game showing that a single-valued concept of strategic stability cannot require an equilibrium to stay stable after deletion of an inferior response. The unique backwards induction equilibrium is (T,R), with payoffs (2,0); but when the inferior response B is deleted (Figure 13), the unique backwards induction equilibrium is (M,L), with payoffs (3,1). The unique stable set of this game includes (T,(1/2,1/2)), at which B is not an inferior response.

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or continue; player II then chooses L, which ends the game, or R; player I then chooses M or B.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 14
games.description:
The stage game of the chain store paradox, an example from information economics due to Kreps, in which stability distinguishes between two components of Nash equilibria that are all sequential, perfect and proper. Only the component in which the chosen player sends a strong signal is stable.

Nature chooses Weak (W) with probability 1/10 or Strong (S) with probability 9/10. The chosen player sends a strong signal s or a weak signal w; a true signal is costless and a false signal costs 1 unit. The Entrant, informed only of the signal, chooses f (fight) or r (retreat). If he fights he wins 1 against Weak and loses 1 against Strong; the signaling player loses 2 whenever there is a fight. Payoffs are in the order Weak, Strong, Entrant.

The Nash equilibria form two connected components: (1) the chosen player sends a strong signal, the Entrant retreats after a strong signal and fights with probability at least 1/2 after a weak signal; (2) the chosen player sends a weak signal, the Entrant retreats after a weak signal and fights with probability at least 1/2 after a strong signal. Component (2) is not stable: sending a strong signal is an inferior response for Weak, and once it is deleted the Entrant's fighting after a strong signal is dominated.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 17
games.description:
A game used to show that requiring sequentiality in every tree with the same reduced normal form is insufficient for strategic stability. Its unique backwards induction equilibrium is (continue, R, B) with payoffs (3,3). If one dummy player per cell of the strategic form is added, each receiving 1 in that cell and 0 otherwise, the equilibrium with payoffs (2,2) (T,R) becomes sequential in every tree with the same reduced normal form, although (3,3) should remain the only strategically stable equilibrium.

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or continue; player II then chooses L, which ends the game, or R; player I then chooses M or B. The paper prints no action labels for this figure; the labels here follow those of Figure 12.

The dummy players of the paper's argument are described only in words and are not included.

The paper prints the matrix without labels. Here the rows are, in the printed order, T, B and M, where B and M are player I's choices at his second move after continue at the first, as in the tree of Figure 17; the columns are L and R.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 2 (x = 0)
games.description:
The game :math:`\Gamma(x)`, showing that conformity with backwards induction is necessary but not sufficient for strategic stability. Player I chooses T, which ends the game, M or B; player II, who is not told whether I chose M or B, chooses L or R.

The equilibrium (T,R) with payoffs (2,2) is sequential, but strategically unstable: B is strictly dominated by T, so if II has to move he should infer that I played M, hence play L, and I should then deviate to M; the unique strategically stable equilibrium is (M,L) with payoffs (3,3). The paper notes that (T,R) is also proper here. The Nash equilibria form two connected components: the singleton (M,L) with payoffs (3,3), and the interval from (T,R) to (T,(2/3,1/3)), with payoffs (2,2).

The parameter x is 0 in this file, the game written :math:`\Gamma(0)` in the paper; the paper allows any :math:`x \le 2`, and uses :math:`1 < x \le 2` in its main discussion.

For x > 1, B is also strictly dominated by M, and for x = 2 player I has the additional, more direct reason to deviate from T that T is dominated by M. The game :math:`\Gamma(x)` with player I's three-way choice coalesced into two binary choices, showing that sequential equilibrium depends on how the tree is drawn. The reduced normal form is the same as that of the game with a single three-way choice, but the equilibrium (T,R) with payoffs (2,2), which is sequential there, behaves differently here.

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or continue; he then chooses M or B; player II, who is not told whether I chose M or B, chooses L or R. In the subgame that starts after continue, both (M,L) with payoffs (3,3) and (B,R) with payoffs (1,1) are strict equilibria, and both are strategically stable in the subgame; but the paper argues, by forward induction, that only the (3,3) equilibrium is part of a strategically stable equilibrium of the whole game.

The parameter x is 0 in this file, the game written :math:`\Gamma(0)` in the paper; the paper allows any :math:`x \le 2`, and uses :math:`1 < x \le 2` in its main discussion.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 4
games.description:
A third presentation of :math:`\Gamma(0)`, the game of Figure 3 with x = 0, in which player I's randomization between T and M is written as a move of nature, showing that adding such a coin toss destroys the sequential equilibrium (T,R) with payoffs (2,2), even though the reduced normal form is unchanged.

At his second information set player I can choose coin, M or B. Choosing coin gives the move to nature, which ends the game with payoffs (2,2) with probability 2/3 (action T) and otherwise leads to II's information set (action M). The choice coin strictly dominates B, so in any sequential equilibrium I chooses coin or M there, II assigns probability zero to the position following B and chooses L, and I chooses M: the only sequential equilibrium is (M,L) with payoffs (3,3).

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 5
games.description:
A game showing that replacing a subgame by its payoff (a form of backwards induction rationality) is incompatible with admissibility. Player I chooses top or bottom, and in each case player II then moves in a separate information set, choosing between up with payoffs (1,1) and down with payoffs (0,0).

If the top subgame is replaced by a terminal position with payoffs (1,1), admissibility forces I to choose top in any solution; by the same argument he must choose bottom, a contradiction. The same example shows that neither perfect nor proper equilibria satisfy this property.

source.title: On the strategic stability of equilibria

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 6
games.description:
A variant of :math:`\Gamma(0)` in which the outcome after B and L is replaced by a zero-sum subgame (matching pennies with payoffs of plus or minus 4), showing that iterated elimination of dominated strategies in the normal form does not by itself yield backwards induction.

Player I chooses T, which ends the game, or continue; he then chooses M or B, and II, not told which, chooses L or R. After B and L, I chooses T or B in the subgame, and II, not told which, chooses L or R. Any dominance relation appears only after the zero-sum subgame has been replaced by its value; all strategies are undominated in the normal form, so the whole strategy space is persistent, and the equilibrium (T,R) with payoffs (2,2) survives that procedure. The unique strategically stable set is (M,L) with payoffs (3,3).

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 6 (normal form)
games.description:
The normal form of the game of Figure 6, a variant of :math:`\Gamma(0)` with a zero-sum subgame, printed beneath the tree. Every strategy is undominated, so iterated elimination of dominated strategies removes nothing, although the equilibrium (T,R) with payoffs (2,2) is not strategically stable.

Player I's strategies are T, M, and BT and BB (B at the second information set, then T or B in the subgame). Player II's strategies LL and LR are L at the first information set followed by L or R in the subgame; R is R at the first information set.

games.title: Kohlberg and Mertens (1986), Figure 7 (alpha = 0)
games.description:
The tree :math:`\Delta(\alpha)`, which has the same reduced normal form as the matrix game :math:`\Delta` for every :math:`0 \le \alpha \le 1`, used to show that the requirement of sequentiality in every equivalent tree may be impossible to satisfy: its unique sequential equilibrium has player II choosing L with probability :math:`(4-3\alpha)/(8-4\alpha)`, which depends on :math:`\alpha`, although all these trees are equivalent.

Player I chooses T, which ends the game with payoffs (1,-1), or X; he then chooses coin, M or B. Choosing coin gives the move to nature, which ends the game with payoffs (1,-1) with probability :math:`\alpha` (action T) and otherwise leads to II's information set (action M, with probability :math:`1-\alpha`). Player II chooses L or R without being told which position he is in.

The paper leaves :math:`\alpha` free; this file uses :math:`\alpha = 0`, an example value chosen for this entry within the paper's range :math:`0 \le \alpha \le 1`. Player II's probability of L in the unique sequential equilibrium is then 1/2.

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 1
games.description:
A game of imperfect information that serves as the running example for the extensive-form
notation. Player 1 chooses A, which ends the game, or L or R, after which Player 2 chooses l or r
without being told whether Player 1 chose L or R. Player 2's information set and the four terminal
nodes that follow it form a nonproper subform, so the game has no proper subgame.

source.title: Sequential equilibria

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 11
games.description:
A three-player game with a complicated set of sequential equilibria. Player 1 chooses A or
chooses one of two bimatrix games, L or R, for Players 2 and 3 to play, and neither Player 2 nor
Player 3 knows which. Payoffs to Players 2 and 3 after L are (1,0) at (l,l') and (r,r'), and
(0,1) at (l,r') and (r,l'); after R they are (1,1) at (l,l'), (0,1) at (r,l'), and (0,0) otherwise.
There are two types of sequential equilibria. In the first, Player 1 plays R and Players 2 and 3
play l and l'. In the second, Player 1 plays A, which leaves Players 2 and 3 free in their
beliefs about whether Player 1 chose L or R; for a sequential equilibrium the common belief that
the node following L has been reached must lie in [1/2, 1/1.1].

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 13
games.description:
A game with a sequential equilibrium that is not perfect: Player 1 plays L and Player 2 plays r.
Here Player 1 chooses L or R and Player 2, not observing the choice, chooses l or r.

source.title: Sequential equilibria

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 14
games.description:
A game, due to Kohlberg, used to show how restrictions on beliefs choose among sequential
equilibria. One sequential equilibrium has Player 1 playing A and Player 2 playing r, supported
by beliefs of Player 2 that the node following L has probability at most 1/2. A second has Player
1 playing L and Player 2 playing l. The paper argues the second is more plausible: R is dominated
by A for Player 1, so Player 2 should not conclude on reaching the information set that Player 1
chose R.

source.title: Sequential equilibria

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Section 8, variant of Figure 14
games.description:
A modification of the game of Figure 14, in which Player 1's choice of A leads to a simultaneous
bimatrix game for Players 1 and 2 instead of ending the game with payoffs (1,1). The paper
argues that there is again a sequential equilibrium in which Player 1 chooses A, supported by
beliefs of Player 2 that the node following L has probability less than 1/2, and that these beliefs
are implausible: A now yields Player 1 an equilibrium payoff of 1, more than Player 1 gets from R,
so Player 2 should not attach much weight to R, which again makes L and l the more plausible
equilibrium.

The paper states that the bimatrix game has a unique Nash equilibrium in which Player 1 receives
1. For the payoffs as printed, the unique equilibrium has Player 1 mixing Top and Bottom with
probability 1/2 each and Player 2 mixing Left and Right with probability 1/2 each, which gives
Player 1 expected payoff -4 (and Player 2 5/2). The payoffs are entered as printed.

The paper gives the modification in words and as a bimatrix, not as a tree. The file encodes the
simultaneous game after A in the usual way: Player 1 chooses Top or Bottom, then Player 2, who
knows that A was chosen but not which row, chooses Left, Middle or Right. These row and column
labels are not in the paper. After L and R the game is as in Figure 14.

games.description:
A perfect-information game used to motivate subgame perfection. Player 1 chooses L, which ends
the game, or R, after which Player 2 chooses l or r. The profile in which Player 1 plays L and
Player 2 plays l is a Nash equilibrium that is not subgame perfect: Player 2's choice is
irrelevant as long as Player 1 plays L, but in the proper subgame after R Player 2 does better by
choosing r, and anticipating this Player 1 should choose R.

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 3: Selten's horse
games.name: Selten's horse
games.description:
A three-player game with no proper subgame, used to motivate beliefs and sequential
rationality. The profile in which Player 1 plays D, Player 2 plays a and Player 3 plays l is
subgame perfect, since the only proper subgame is the game itself, but it is not sensible:
Player 2's information set is a singleton, and given Player 3's choice of l Player 2 prefers d at
it, after which Player 1 would do better by choosing A rather than D. The only sensible
equilibrium has Player 1 choosing A, Player 2 choosing a, and Player 3 choosing r with
probability at least 3/4.

See also (Selten 1975)
    The same game and payoffs, with the actions labeled R and L.

R, Player 2 does better by choosing l, and anticipating this Player 1 chooses L.

games.title: Kreps and Wilson (1982), Figure 8
games.description:
A game with a Nash equilibrium that is extended subgame perfect but cannot be part of any
sequential equilibrium. The information sets are arranged so that the only subform is the whole
game, so every Nash equilibrium is extended subgame perfect. The profile in which Player 1 plays
a, Player 2 plays A and Player 3 plays a' (the strategies marked (1) in the paper's figure) is a
Nash equilibrium, but whatever beliefs Player 2 holds at the information set, B is better than A
for Player 2, and if Player 2 plays B then Players 1 and 3 prefer b and b'.

The paper's game has two initial nodes, each with probability 1/2: at one Player 1 moves first,
at the other Player 3 moves first. The file represents them with a chance node whose branches are
labeled by who moves first.

Players 1 and 2 alternate, Player 1 moving first, with seven decision nodes. Player 1's continuing moves are unlabeled in the paper and are called continue here.

Player 1 chooses a or continue; if Player 1 continues, Player 2 chooses d or continue; after both continue, Player 1 (b or c) and Player 2 (e or f) play a simultaneous-move game, so Player 2's second information set contains both of Player 1's choices. games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 1(c)
games.description:
Reduced normal form of a game in which player 1 chooses between an outside option l, with payoffs (2,5), and r, after which the battle of the sexes of Figure 1(a) is played; player 2 learns only that l was not chosen. Strategy rs means r followed by s, and rw means r followed by w. The paper also draws the tree schematically (Figure 1(b)), with BS as a box; it is not entered.

The equilibrium in which player 1 takes l, and the players would continue with (w,s) if BS were reached, is perfect but not stable: rw is weakly dominated, so player 2 should conclude after r that player 1 plays rs and respond with w; iterated elimination of weakly dominated strategies leaves only the outcome (3,1). This is the forward induction argument of Kohlberg and Mertens.

source.title: Stable equilibria and forward induction

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 2 (epsilon = 1/10)
games.description:
The normal form of the game of Figure 1(b) (the outside option l against the battle of the sexes) when player 1's plan l is perturbed in the extensive form: with probability :math:`\epsilon` player 1 mistakenly chooses r, after which the planned choice s or w is played in the battle of the sexes. Strategy ls means plan l and, if r is chosen by mistake, s; likewise lw, rs and rw. Then ls and lw are no longer equivalent, and for every :math:`\epsilon > 0` the profile (lw,s) is a strict, hence stable, equilibrium. It corresponds to the perfect but unstable equilibrium in which player 1 takes l, so perfectness with independent mistakes and Kohlberg-Mertens stability differ.

The paper leaves :math:`\epsilon` a small positive number; this file uses :math:`\epsilon = 1/10`, an example value chosen for this entry. The paper prints the entries of the l rows as expressions in :math:`\epsilon`.

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 3(a)
games.description:
The zero-sum game whose strategic form is Figure 3(b). Player 1 chooses D, ending the game, or A; after A, player 2 chooses d, ending the game, or a, after which player 1 chooses delta or alpha. In the paper the last two actions are written with the Greek letters delta and alpha.

Player 1 plays D in any Nash equilibrium, so player 2 moves only after a deviation. Subgame perfectness requires player 2 to believe that player 1 would then play delta, but stability does not: the unique stable set includes both (D,d) and (D, a mixture of d and a), so a stable set can contain more outcomes than survive iterated elimination of dominated strategies.

source.title: Stable equilibria and forward induction

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 3(b)
games.description:

Player 1 plays D in every Nash equilibrium, so the subgame perfect equilibrium in which player 2 then plays d if reached relies on player 2 believing that player 1 would play delta rather than alpha. The unique stable set contains both (D,d) and (D, a mixture of d and a) for player 2, so a stable set can contain more outcomes than survive iterated elimination of dominated strategies.

Player 1's strategies are D, and delta or alpha at the second node after A and a; the labels are the paper's.

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 4(b)
games.description:
Reduced normal form of a game in which player 1 chooses between an outside option l, with payoffs (2,2), and r, after which player 1 and player 2 play a 2 x 3 simultaneous-move subgame (player 1 chooses T or B, player 2 chooses L, M or R); strategy rT means r followed by T. The paper also draws the tree schematically (Figure 4(a)), with the subgame as a matrix; it is not entered.

The paper uses the game to show that a stable equilibrium need not be self-enforcing. By a forward induction argument only (rT,L), a strict equilibrium, is self-enforcing, since choosing the subgame signals that player 1 will play T. Yet the equilibrium component in which player 1 chooses l with probability one, with outcome (2,2), is also stable.

games.description:

Only the reduced normal form is printed, so no tree is given. Player 1's strategies are os and ow (do not burn, then play s or w) and xs and xw (burn x, then play s or w); player 2's strategy is a pair whose first letter is the action if player 1 did not burn and whose second letter is the action if player 1 burned.

For 1/4 < x < 2, iterated elimination of dominated strategies leaves a unique outcome: player 1 does not burn money and plays s, and player 2 plays w, giving (3,1). The paper takes x > 1/4 and notes that if 1 <= x <= 2 all the dominations are by pure strategies.

The file uses x = 1, a value in that range chosen for this entry.

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 6
games.description:
The reduced game of the twofold repetition of the battle of the sexes, after eliminating strategies that are inferior responses to the equilibrium component in which (s,w) is played twice. A strategy of player 1, such as (s,ws), gives the round 1 action and then the round 2 actions after player 2 played s and w in round 1; a strategy of player 2 such as (s,w.) gives the round 1 action and the round 2 reaction to player 1's s, the reaction to w being irrelevant and omitted (written as a dot).

(s,w.) is an inferior response against the component with payoff (6,2), and once it is deleted, (s,ss) becomes dominated. Iterated elimination then leaves (1,3), which is not in the component, so the path in which (3,1) is played twice is not stable.

games.title: van Damme (1989), Figure 7 (a = 3/2)
games.description:
A modified battle of the sexes in which the payoff to both players from (w,w) is a, used to show that stable paths of the twofold repetition need not alternate between the players' most preferred equilibria. For a < 3 the game has three stable equilibria: (s,w), (w,s), and a completely mixed equilibrium. If 1 < a < 2, then in the twofold repetition the alternating paths between (3,1) and (1,3) are not stable either, so all stable paths involve randomization at stage 1 and all stable equilibria are inefficient. If 2 < a < 5/2, the path (s,w), (s,w) is unstable yet is immune against any convincing deviation in the sense of Osborne.

The paper leaves a general; this file uses a = 3/2, an example value chosen for this entry, in the range 1 < a < 2.

games.title: Harsanyi (1968), Section 10
games.description:
A two-person zero-sum Bayesian game that illustrates exploiting an opponent's erroneous beliefs.
The payoffs are those of the Section 9 example (attribute classes a1, a2 for Player 1 and b1, b2 for
Player 2, each player knowing only his own class), but chance now draws the pair of classes with
probabilities (a1,b1) 0.01, (a1,b2) 0.00, (a2,b1) 0.09 and (a2,b2) 0.90. Player 1 in class a1 is
therefore sure that Player 2 is in b1, while Player 2 in class b1 assigns probability 0.90 to the
mistaken hypothesis that Player 1 is in a2. The unique saddle point of the normal form has
Player 1 playing y2 in class a1 and y1 in class a2 and Player 2 playing z2 in b1 and z1 in b2;
by playing y2 against the z2 that Player 2 expects, Player 1 in class a1 exploits the mistake and
obtains 20 instead of 2 or 5. The probability 0.00 for (a1,b2) is kept as a chance branch.

One entry of the paper's normal form (Table 21) differs from the value these payoffs imply; see that entry.

games.title: Harsanyi (1968), Section 9
games.description:
A two-person zero-sum Bayesian game with incomplete information, used to illustrate that a
Bayesian equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of the normal form of the game. Player 1 belongs to
attribute class a1 ("weak") or a2 ("strong") and Player 2 to class b1 ("weak") or b2 ("strong");
each player knows only his own class. Chance draws the pair of classes with the joint
probabilities of the paper: (a1,b1) 0.40, (a1,b2) 0.10, (a2,b1) 0.20, (a2,b2) 0.30. Player 1 then
chooses y1 or y2 and Player 2 chooses z1 or z2, each at one information set per own class, so
neither observes the other's class or move. Payoffs are to Player 1, with Player 2 receiving the
negative. Each of the four payoff matrices has a pure saddle point: (y1,z1) for (a1,b1), (y2,z1)
for (a1,b2), (y1,z2) for (a2,b1) and (y1,z1) for (a2,b2). The normal form has a unique saddle
point, in which Player 1 plays y2 if in a1 and y1 if in a2, and Player 2 plays z1 whatever his
class, which differs from the optimal strategies of the separate matrices.

The caption of the matrix for (a1,b1) is misprinted in the paper as (a2,b1); the text and the
normal form show that it belongs to (a1,b1).

source.title: Games with incomplete information played by ``Bayesian'' players, I--III. Part II. Bayesian equilibrium points

games.title: Harsanyi (1968), Section 9, counterexample

have the maximin property in terms of his conditional payoffs. The structure is that of Section 9
(attribute classes a1, a2 for Player 1 and b1, b2 for Player 2, each player knowing only his own),
with the four payoff matrices of the paper and all four pairs of classes having probability 0.25.
Payoffs are to Player 1, with Player 2 receiving the negative. The pure saddle points of the
matrices are (y2,z2) for (a1,b1), (y2,z1) for (a1,b2), (y1,z1) for (a2,b1) and (y1,z2) for
(a2,b2). The only saddle point of the normal form is (y11,z11), in which Player 1 plays y1 in both
classes and Player 2 plays z1 in both. In class a1 Player 1's best reply to z11 is y1, but y2
maximizes his security level in terms of his conditional payoffs.

games.title: Cho and Kreps (1987), Figure I: Beer-Quiche game
games.name: Beer-Quiche game
games.description:
A signaling game that shows how restrictions on out-of-equilibrium beliefs can eliminate
equilibria. Player A, the sender, is a wimp with probability 0.1 or surly with probability 0.9 and
knows which; A chooses beer or quiche for breakfast. Player B, the receiver, observes the breakfast
but not the type and chooses whether to duel. The wimp prefers quiche and the surly prefers beer,
each worth an increment of 1 to A; A gets a further 2 if B does not duel, and B wants to duel
only if A is a wimp. There are two equilibrium outcomes, both sequential, in which A has beer
whatever his type or quiche whatever his type. The argument of the paper rules out the second:
if the equilibrium meal is quiche, a wimp cannot gain from beer but a surly A could, so B should
not believe that beer comes from a wimp, and B would not duel after beer. The equilibrium in which
both types have beer is unbroken by this argument, since there it is the wimp, not the surly, who
could gain from a defection to quiche.

source.title: Signaling games and stable equilibria

games.title: Cho and Kreps (1987), Figure II
games.description:
A variation of the Beer-Quiche game of Figure I in which B has a third option, to give A
$1,000,000. Giving away the million is always a dominated strategy for B, so the set of equilibria
is unchanged. But the option defeats the specific argument against the equilibrium in which both
types have quiche: after an out-of-equilibrium meal of beer, B can no longer rule out that the
wimp sent it, since the wimp too could conceivably benefit from the defection. The prior (wimp 0.1,
surly 0.9) and the duel and don't payoffs are those of Figure I. The action labelled give 1M is the
paper's give $1M.

source.title: Signaling games and stable equilibria

games.title: Cho and Kreps (1987), Figure III
games.description:
A signaling game that shows that tests based on dominance of type-message pairs eliminate an
equilibrium outcome that trembling-hand perfection and properness do not. Player A, the sender,
has type t1 with probability 0.9 or t2 with probability 0.1 and knows which. A sends message m,
which ends the game with payoffs (0,0), or m', after which B, not knowing the type, chooses r1 or
r2. Consider the equilibrium outcome in which both types send m and B responds to m' with r1 with
probability at least 0.5. To support it B must put weight at least 0.5 on t2 after m', but for t2
the message m dominates m'. Pruning the pair (t2,m') leaves B no choice but to respond to m' with
r2, which makes t1 defect, so the outcome fails the paper's tests. The equilibrium in which A sends
m regardless of type and B responds to m' with r1 is nevertheless proper, and perfect in the agent
normal form.
